Medium 969. Pancake Sorting Amazon Array

Problem: Sort a permutation of 1..n using prefix reversals (flip the first k elements). Return any sequence of ks with at most 10n flips.

Solve it on LeetCode ↗

Example 1
Input: arr = [3,2,4,1]
Output: [4,2,4,3]
Explanation: We perform 4 pancake flips, with k values 4, 2, 4, and 3. Starting state: arr = [3, 2, 4, 1] After 1st flip (k = 4): arr = [1, 4, 2, 3] After 2nd flip (k = 2): arr = [4, 1, 2, 3] After 3rd flip (k = 4): arr = [3, 2, 1, 4] After 4th flip (k = 3): arr = [1, 2, 3, 4], which is sorted.
Example 2
Input: arr = [1,2,3]
Output: []
Explanation: The input is already sorted, so there is no need to flip anything. Note that other answers, such as [3, 3], would also be accepted.

Constraints: 1 ≤ arr.length ≤ 100 · 1 ≤ arr[i] ≤ arr.length · All integers in arr are unique (i.e. arr is a permutation of the integers from 1 to arr.length).

Hint 1

Put the largest pancake at the bottom first.

Hint 2

How do you move any pancake to the top with one flip?

From brute force to the pattern: Searching for the minimum flips is exponential; two flips per value is O(n²) and valid.

Spot it: Place values from largest to smallest: each takes two flips (to the front, then to the back of the unsorted part) — a two-pointer reversal pattern.

Why not another pattern? Searching for the fewest flips is NP-hard; the problem only asks for any sequence within 10n.

Approach:

  1. For size from n down to 2: find the index i of size.
  2. Flip i + 1 (it goes to the front), then flip size (it goes to position size − 1).
class Solution:
    def pancakeSort(self, arr: List[int]) -> List[int]:
        flips = []
        for size in range(len(arr), 1, -1):
            i = arr.index(size)  # where the largest unsorted pancake is
            if i == size - 1:
                continue  # already in place
            if i > 0:
                arr[:i + 1] = arr[:i + 1][::-1]  # bring it to the top
                flips.append(i + 1)
            arr[:size] = arr[:size][::-1]  # flip it down into place
            flips.append(size)
        return flips
function pancakeSort(arr: number[]): number[] {
    // reverse arr[0 .. count-1] in place
    function flip(count: number): void {
        let left = 0;
        let right = count - 1;
        while (left < right) {
            [arr[left], arr[right]] = [arr[right], arr[left]];
            left++;
            right--;
        }
    }
    const flips: number[] = [];
    for (let size = arr.length; size > 1; size--) {
        const i = arr.indexOf(size);  // where the largest unsorted pancake is
        if (i === size - 1) {
            continue;  // already in place
        }
        if (i > 0) {
            flip(i + 1);  // bring it to the top
            flips.push(i + 1);
        }
        flip(size);  // flip it down into place
        flips.push(size);
    }
    return flips;
}
class Solution {
    public List<Integer> pancakeSort(int[] arr) {
        List<Integer> flips = new ArrayList<>();
        for (int size = arr.length; size > 1; size--) {
            int i = 0;
            while (arr[i] != size) {
                i++;  // where the largest unsorted pancake is
            }
            if (i == size - 1) {
                continue;  // already in place
            }
            if (i > 0) {
                flip(arr, i + 1);  // bring it to the top
                flips.add(i + 1);
            }
            flip(arr, size);  // flip it down into place
            flips.add(size);
        }
        return flips;
    }

    // reverse arr[0 .. count-1] in place
    private void flip(int[] arr, int count) {
        int left = 0;
        int right = count - 1;
        while (left < right) {
            int temp = arr[left];
            arr[left] = arr[right];
            arr[right] = temp;
            left++;
            right--;
        }
    }
}

What the code is doing, line by line:

  1. After processing size, the last n − size + 1 positions hold their final values.
  2. At most two flips per value: 2n ≤ 10n.

Dry run: use the Step through the solution player under the code. It runs this exact code on Example 1 and shows every line with the variables at that moment.

Edge cases to test:

  • Already sorted → [].
  • Reversed array.
  • n = 1.

Complexity: O(n²) time, O(n) space for the answer.

Medium 1574. Shortest Subarray to be Removed to Make Array Sorted Amazon Array

Problem: Remove one subarray (possibly empty) so the rest is non-decreasing. Return the shortest such removal.

Solve it on LeetCode ↗

Example 1
Input: arr = [1,2,3,10,4,2,3,5]
Output: 3
Explanation: The shortest subarray we can remove is [10,4,2] of length 3. The remaining elements after that will be [1,2,3,3,5] which are sorted. Another correct solution is to remove the subarray [3,10,4].
Example 2
Input: arr = [5,4,3,2,1]
Output: 4
Explanation: Since the array is strictly decreasing, we can only keep a single element. Therefore we need to remove a subarray of length 4, either [5,4,3,2] or [4,3,2,1].

Constraints: 1 ≤ arr.length ≤ 10⁵ · 0 ≤ arr[i] ≤ 10⁹

Hint 1

What does the array look like after the removal?

Hint 2

Fix the sorted suffix, then extend the prefix with a second pointer.

From brute force to the pattern: Every removal + check is O(n³); binary search on the suffix is O(n log n); two pointers is O(n).

Spot it: What remains is a sorted prefix plus a sorted suffix. Find the longest sorted suffix starting at r; then for each prefix end l, move r forward until arr[r] ≥ arr[l] — two pointers, both only moving right.

Why not another pattern? Trying every removal and checking sortedness is O(n³).

Approach:

  1. r = start of the longest non-decreasing suffix. If r == 0, return 0.
  2. Answer starts as r (remove the whole prefix).
  3. For l = 0, 1, … while the prefix stays sorted: advance r while arr[r] < arr[l]; candidate r − l − 1.
class Solution:
    def findLengthOfShortestSubarray(self, arr: List[int]) -> int:
        n = len(arr)
        r = n - 1
        while r > 0 and arr[r - 1] <= arr[r]:
            r -= 1  # longest sorted suffix starts at r
        if r == 0:
            return 0  # already sorted
        best = r  # remove everything before the suffix
        for l in range(n):
            if l > 0 and arr[l] < arr[l - 1]:
                break  # the prefix is no longer sorted
            while r < n and arr[r] < arr[l]:
                r += 1  # suffix must start at a value >= arr[l]
            best = min(best, r - l - 1)  # remove arr[l+1 .. r-1]
        return best
function findLengthOfShortestSubarray(arr: number[]): number {
    const n = arr.length;
    let r = n - 1;
    while (r > 0 && arr[r - 1] <= arr[r]) {
        r -= 1;  // longest sorted suffix starts at r
    }
    if (r === 0) {
        return 0;  // already sorted
    }
    let best = r;  // remove everything before the suffix
    for (let l = 0; l < n; l++) {
        if (l > 0 && arr[l] < arr[l - 1]) {
            break;  // the prefix is no longer sorted
        }
        while (r < n && arr[r] < arr[l]) {
            r += 1;  // suffix must start at a value >= arr[l]
        }
        best = Math.min(best, r - l - 1);  // remove arr[l+1 .. r-1]
    }
    return best;
}
class Solution {
    public int findLengthOfShortestSubarray(int[] arr) {
        int n = arr.length;
        int r = n - 1;
        while (r > 0 && arr[r - 1] <= arr[r]) {
            r -= 1;  // longest sorted suffix starts at r
        }
        if (r == 0) {
            return 0;  // already sorted
        }
        int best = r;  // remove everything before the suffix
        for (int l = 0; l < n; l++) {
            if (l > 0 && arr[l] < arr[l - 1]) {
                break;  // the prefix is no longer sorted
            }
            while (r < n && arr[r] < arr[l]) {
                r += 1;  // suffix must start at a value >= arr[l]
            }
            best = Math.min(best, r - l - 1);  // remove arr[l+1 .. r-1]
        }
        return best;
    }
}

What the code is doing, line by line:

  1. The kept prefix must be sorted and the kept suffix must be sorted, and the junction must not decrease.
  2. As l grows, arr[l] grows, so the needed r never moves back.

Dry run: use the Step through the solution player under the code. It runs this exact code on Example 1 and shows every line with the variables at that moment.

Edge cases to test:

  • Already sorted → 0.
  • Strictly decreasing → n − 1.
  • Equal values.

Complexity: O(n) time, O(1) space.

Medium 1679. Max Number of K-Sum Pairs Amazon ArrayHash Map

Problem: Repeatedly remove two numbers summing to k. Return the maximum number of removals.

Solve it on LeetCode ↗

Example 1
Input: nums = [1,2,3,4], k = 5
Output: 2
Explanation: Starting with nums = [1,2,3,4]: - Remove numbers 1 and 4, then nums = [2,3] - Remove numbers 2 and 3, then nums = [] There are no more pairs that sum up to 5, hence a total of 2 operations.
Example 2
Input: nums = [3,1,3,4,3], k = 6
Output: 1
Explanation: Starting with nums = [3,1,3,4,3]: - Remove the first two 3's, then nums = [1,4,3] There are no more pairs that sum up to 6, hence a total of 1 operation.

Constraints: 1 ≤ nums.length ≤ 10⁵ · 1 ≤ nums[i] ≤ 10⁹ · 1 ≤ k ≤ 10⁹

Hint 1

Sort the array.

Hint 2

Use two pointers from both ends, as in Two Sum II.

From brute force to the pattern: Nested loops are O(n²); sort + two pointers is O(n log n).

Spot it: Pairs with a fixed sum → sort + two pointers from both ends (or a hash map of unmatched values).

Why not another pattern? Greedy pairing in arbitrary order with nested loops is O(n²).

Approach:

  1. Sort.
  2. l, r at the ends: equal to k → count, move both; less → l += 1; more → r −= 1.
class Solution:
    def maxOperations(self, nums: List[int], k: int) -> int:
        nums = sorted(nums)
        l, r = 0, len(nums) - 1
        pairs = 0
        while l < r:
            s = nums[l] + nums[r]
            if s == k:
                pairs += 1  # use both
                l += 1
                r -= 1
            elif s < k:
                l += 1  # need a bigger sum
            else:
                r -= 1  # need a smaller sum
        return pairs
function maxOperations(nums: number[], k: number): number {
    nums = [...nums].sort((a, b) => a - b);
    let l = 0;
    let r = nums.length - 1;
    let pairs = 0;
    while (l < r) {
        const s = nums[l] + nums[r];
        if (s === k) {
            pairs += 1;  // use both
            l += 1;
            r -= 1;
        } else if (s < k) {
            l += 1;  // need a bigger sum
        } else {
            r -= 1;  // need a smaller sum
        }
    }
    return pairs;
}
class Solution {
    public int maxOperations(int[] nums, int k) {
        nums = nums.clone();
        Arrays.sort(nums);
        int l = 0;
        int r = nums.length - 1;
        int pairs = 0;
        while (l < r) {
            int s = nums[l] + nums[r];
            if (s == k) {
                pairs += 1;  // use both
                l += 1;
                r -= 1;
            } else if (s < k) {
                l += 1;  // need a bigger sum
            } else {
                r -= 1;  // need a smaller sum
            }
        }
        return pairs;
    }
}

What the code is doing, line by line:

  1. In a sorted array, if nums[l] + nums[r] < k, nums[l] can't pair with anything left, so it's discarded.
  2. Pairing a matching couple never hurts the maximum (exchange argument).

Dry run: use the Step through the solution player under the code. It runs this exact code on Example 1 and shows every line with the variables at that moment.

Edge cases to test:

  • Duplicates (k = 2x).
  • No pairs → 0.
  • All pairs.

Complexity: O(n log n) time, O(n) space (or O(n) time with a hash map).

Medium 2161. Partition Array According to Given Pivot Amazon Microsoft Array

Problem: Rearrange so values < pivot come first, then == pivot, then > pivot, keeping the relative order inside each group.

Solve it on LeetCode ↗

Example 1
Input: nums = [9,12,5,10,14,3,10], pivot = 10
Output: [9,5,3,10,10,12,14]
Explanation: The elements 9, 5, and 3 are less than the pivot so they are on the left side of the array. The elements 12 and 14 are greater than the pivot so they are on the right side of the array. The relative ordering of the elements less than and greater than pivot is also maintained. [9, 5, 3] and [12, 14] are the respective orderings.
Example 2
Input: nums = [-3,4,3,2], pivot = 2
Output: [-3,2,4,3]
Explanation: The element -3 is less than the pivot so it is on the left side of the array. The elements 4 and 3 are greater than the pivot so they are on the right side of the array. The relative ordering of the elements less than and greater than pivot is also maintained. [-3] and [4, 3] are the respective orderings.

Constraints: 1 ≤ nums.length ≤ 10⁵ · -10⁶ ≤ nums[i] ≤ 10⁶ · pivot equals to an element of nums.

Hint 1

Why doesn't the in-place Dutch flag algorithm work here?

Hint 2

Write the small values from the front and the large ones from the back.

From brute force to the pattern: Three separate list passes are also O(n); the two-pointer version does it in one.

Spot it: A three-way partition, but stable. In-place swapping (Dutch flag) breaks the order, so fill the result with two pointers: smaller values from the front, larger values from the back (reading the array backwards), pivots in between.

Why not another pattern? The Dutch national flag swap scheme is O(1) space but not stable.

Approach:

  1. lo writes smaller values from the left (scan forward); hi writes larger values from the right (scan backward).
  2. Fill the gap between them with pivot.
class Solution:
    def pivotArray(self, nums: List[int], pivot: int) -> List[int]:
        n = len(nums)
        result = [pivot] * n  # anything not overwritten is the pivot
        lo, hi = 0, n - 1
        for i in range(n):
            if nums[i] < pivot:
                result[lo] = nums[i]  # smaller values, in order, from the left
                lo += 1
            if nums[n - 1 - i] > pivot:
                result[hi] = nums[n - 1 - i]  # larger values, scanned backwards, from the right
                hi -= 1
        return result
function pivotArray(nums: number[], pivot: number): number[] {
    const n = nums.length;
    const result: number[] = new Array(n).fill(pivot);  // anything not overwritten is the pivot
    let lo = 0;
    let hi = n - 1;
    for (let i = 0; i < n; i++) {
        if (nums[i] < pivot) {
            result[lo] = nums[i];  // smaller values, in order, from the left
            lo += 1;
        }
        if (nums[n - 1 - i] > pivot) {
            result[hi] = nums[n - 1 - i];  // larger values, scanned backwards, from the right
            hi -= 1;
        }
    }
    return result;
}
class Solution {
    public int[] pivotArray(int[] nums, int pivot) {
        int n = nums.length;
        int[] result = new int[n];
        Arrays.fill(result, pivot);  // anything not overwritten is the pivot
        int lo = 0;
        int hi = n - 1;
        for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) {
            if (nums[i] < pivot) {
                result[lo] = nums[i];  // smaller values, in order, from the left
                lo += 1;
            }
            if (nums[n - 1 - i] > pivot) {
                result[hi] = nums[n - 1 - i];  // larger values, scanned backwards, from the right
                hi -= 1;
            }
        }
        return result;
    }
}

What the code is doing, line by line:

  1. Scanning backwards while writing backwards keeps the larger values in their original order.
  2. Pre-filling with pivot handles the middle group automatically.

Dry run: use the Step through the solution player under the code. It runs this exact code on Example 1 and shows every line with the variables at that moment.

Edge cases to test:

  • Pivot appears many times.
  • All smaller or all larger.
  • Negative numbers.

Complexity: O(n) time, O(n) space for the result.

Medium 2938. Separate Black and White Balls Amazon String

Problem: Group all 1s to the right and 0s to the left using adjacent swaps. Return the minimum number of swaps.

Solve it on LeetCode ↗

Example 1
Input: s = "101"
Output: 1
Explanation: We can group all the black balls to the right in the following way: - Swap s[0] and s[1], s = "011". Initially, 1s are not grouped together, requiring at least 1 step to group them to the right.
Example 2
Input: s = "100"
Output: 2
Explanation: We can group all the black balls to the right in the following way: - Swap s[0] and s[1], s = "010". - Swap s[1] and s[2], s = "001". It can be proven that the minimum number of steps needed is 2.

Constraints: 1 ≤ n == s.length ≤ 10⁵ · s[i] is either '0' or '1'.

Hint 1

What does one adjacent swap of a 1 and a 0 achieve?

Hint 2

Count inversions: pairs (1 before 0).

From brute force to the pattern: Bubble-sort simulation is O(n²); counting is O(n).

Spot it: Each adjacent swap moves one 0 past one 1. So the answer is the number of (1, 0) pairs in order — count 1s seen so far while scanning (a two-pointer / counting idea: the next 0 goes to the next free left slot).

Why not another pattern? Simulating swaps (bubble sort) is O(n²).

Approach:

  1. ones = 0; for each character: 1 → ones += 1; 0 → swaps += ones.
class Solution:
    def minimumSteps(self, s: str) -> int:
        swaps = 0
        ones = 0  # black balls to the left of the current position
        for ch in s:
            if ch == "1":
                ones += 1
            else:
                swaps += ones  # this white ball must pass every black ball before it
        return swaps
function minimumSteps(s: string): number {
    let swaps = 0;
    let ones = 0;  // black balls to the left of the current position
    for (const ch of s) {
        if (ch === "1") {
            ones += 1;
        } else {
            swaps += ones;  // this white ball must pass every black ball before it
        }
    }
    return swaps;
}
class Solution {
    public long minimumSteps(String s) {
        long swaps = 0;
        long ones = 0;  // black balls to the left of the current position
        for (char ch : s.toCharArray()) {
            if (ch == '1') {
                ones += 1;
            } else {
                swaps += ones;  // this white ball must pass every black ball before it
            }
        }
        return swaps;
    }
}

What the code is doing, line by line:

  1. Every out-of-order pair needs exactly one swap, and each swap fixes exactly one pair.
  2. The answer can exceed 32 bits (n up to 10⁵).

Dry run: use the Step through the solution player under the code. It runs this exact code on Example 1 and shows every line with the variables at that moment.

Edge cases to test:

  • Already separated → 0.
  • All ones or all zeros.
  • Alternating pattern.

Complexity: O(n) time, O(1) space.

Medium 3752. Lexicographically Smallest Negated Permutation that Sums to Target Amazon ArrayMath

Problem: Build the lexicographically smallest array whose absolute values are a permutation of 1..n and whose sum is target, or [].

Solve it on LeetCode ↗

Example 1
Input: n = 3, target = 0
Output: [-3,1,2]
Explanation: The arrays that sum to 0 and whose absolute values form a permutation of size 3 are: [-3, 1, 2] [-3, 2, 1] [-2, -1, 3] [-2, 3, -1] [-1, -2, 3] [-1, 3, -2] [1, -3, 2] [1, 2, -3] [2, -3, 1] [2, 1, -3] [3, -2, -1] [3, -1, -2] The lexicographically smallest one is [-3, 1, 2].
Example 2
Input: n = 1, target = 10000000000
Output: []
Explanation: There are no arrays that sum to 10000000000 and whose absolute values form a permutation of size 1. Therefore, the answer is [].

Constraints: 1 ≤ n ≤ 10⁵ · -10¹⁰ ≤ target ≤ 10¹⁰

Hint 1

How does negating some numbers change the total?

Hint 2

Which numbers should be negated to make the array start as small as possible?

From brute force to the pattern: All 2ⁿ sign choices vs a greedy pick from the top.

Spot it: Starting from 1 + … + n = S, negating a set N changes the sum to S − 2 · sum(N), so sum(N) = (S − target) / 2. To be lexicographically smallest, the array should start with the most negative numbers: greedily put the largest values into N, then sort.

Why not another pattern? Trying all 2ⁿ sign patterns is exponential.

Approach:

  1. S = n(n + 1)/2. If S − target is odd or outside [0, 2S], return [].
  2. T = (S − target)/2; for v = n … 1: if v ≤ T, negate it and T −= v.
  3. Return the values sorted ascending.
class Solution:
    def lexSmallestNegatedPerm(self, n: int, target: int) -> List[int]:
        total = n * (n + 1) // 2
        if (total - target) % 2 or not (-total <= target <= total):
            return []  # the negated part would need a non-integer or impossible sum
        need = (total - target) // 2  # sum of the values we negate
        values = []
        for v in range(n, 0, -1):
            if v <= need:
                values.append(-v)  # negate the biggest values first
                need -= v
            else:
                values.append(v)
        return sorted(values)
function lexSmallestNegatedPerm(n: number, target: number): number[] {
    const total = (n * (n + 1)) / 2;
    if ((total - target) % 2 !== 0 || !(-total <= target && target <= total)) {
        return [];  // the negated part would need a non-integer or impossible sum
    }
    let need = (total - target) / 2;  // sum of the values we negate
    const values: number[] = [];
    for (let v = n; v > 0; v--) {
        if (v <= need) {
            values.push(-v);  // negate the biggest values first
            need -= v;
        } else {
            values.push(v);
        }
    }
    return values.sort((a, b) => a - b);
}
class Solution {
    public int[] lexSmallestNegatedPerm(int n, long target) {
        long total = (long) n * (n + 1) / 2;
        if ((total - target) % 2 != 0 || !(-total <= target && target <= total)) {
            return new int[0];  // the negated part would need a non-integer or impossible sum
        }
        long need = (total - target) / 2;  // sum of the values we negate
        int[] values = new int[n];
        int k = 0;
        for (int v = n; v > 0; v--) {
            if (v <= need) {
                values[k++] = -v;  // negate the biggest values first
                need -= v;
            } else {
                values[k++] = v;
            }
        }
        Arrays.sort(values);
        return values;
    }
}

What the code is doing, line by line:

  1. Any T between 0 and S is a subset sum of 1..n, and taking the largest value that fits always leaves a reachable remainder.
  2. Sorted ascending, the array starts with −(largest negated); making that as large as possible makes the first element as small as possible, and the same for the next ones.

Dry run: use the Step through the solution player under the code. It runs this exact code on Example 1 and shows every line with the variables at that moment.

Edge cases to test:

  • Target out of range → [].
  • Wrong parity → [].
  • Target equals the full sum (nothing negated).

Complexity: O(n log n) time (O(n) without the final sort, since the order is known), O(n) space.

Medium 809. Expressive Words Cisco String

Problem: A word is stretchy if extending some of its letter groups to length ≥ 3 makes it equal to s. Count stretchy words.

Solve it on LeetCode ↗

Example 1
Input: s = "heeellooo", words = ["hello", "hi", "helo"]
Output: 1
Explanation: We can extend "e" and "o" in the word "hello" to get "heeellooo". We can't extend "helo" to get "heeellooo" because the group "ll" is not size 3 or more.
Example 2
Input: s = "zzzzzyyyyy", words = ["zzyy","zy","zyy"]
Output: 3

Constraints: 1 ≤ s.length, words.length ≤ 100 · 1 ≤ words[i].length ≤ 100 · s and words[i] consist of lowercase letters.

Hint 1

Compare the strings group by group.

Hint 2

When is it allowed for s's group to be longer than the word's?

From brute force to the pattern: Trying stretch combinations is exponential; comparing runs is linear.

Spot it: Walk s and a word with two pointers, run by run. Runs must have the same letter, and the s run must equal the word's run or be at least 3 and not shorter.

Why not another pattern? Generating all stretched versions of a word is exponential.

Approach:

  1. runs(x) = list of (letter, length).
  2. A word matches if it has the same letters in order and for each run: ls == lw or (ls ≥ 3 and ls ≥ lw).
from itertools import groupby

class Solution:
    def expressiveWords(self, s: str, words: List[str]) -> int:
        def runs(x):
            return [(ch, len(list(g))) for ch, g in groupby(x)]

        target = runs(s)

        def stretchy(word):
            r = runs(word)
            if len(r) != len(target):
                return False
            for (c1, n1), (c2, n2) in zip(target, r):  # walk both run lists together
                if c1 != c2 or n1 < n2 or (n1 != n2 and n1 < 3):
                    return False  # different letter, too short, or an extension shorter than 3
            return True

        return sum(stretchy(w) for w in words)
function expressiveWords(s: string, words: string[]): number {
    // "heeello" -> [["h", 1], ["e", 3], ["l", 2], ["o", 1]]
    function runs(x: string): [string, number][] {
        const out: [string, number][] = [];
        for (const ch of x) {
            if (out.length > 0 && out[out.length - 1][0] === ch) {
                out[out.length - 1][1] += 1;
            } else {
                out.push([ch, 1]);
            }
        }
        return out;
    }

    const target = runs(s);

    function stretchy(word: string): boolean {
        const r = runs(word);
        if (r.length !== target.length) {
            return false;
        }
        for (let i = 0; i < r.length; i++) {  // walk both run lists together
            const [c1, n1] = target[i];
            const [c2, n2] = r[i];
            if (c1 !== c2 || n1 < n2 || (n1 !== n2 && n1 < 3)) {
                return false;  // different letter, too short, or an extension shorter than 3
            }
        }
        return true;
    }

    let count = 0;
    for (const w of words) {
        if (stretchy(w)) {
            count += 1;
        }
    }
    return count;
}
class Solution {
    public int expressiveWords(String s, String[] words) {
        List<int[]> target = runs(s);
        int count = 0;
        for (String w : words) {
            if (stretchy(target, w)) {
                count += 1;
            }
        }
        return count;
    }

    // "heeello" -> [h,1] [e,3] [l,2] [o,1]  (each run as (letter, length))
    private List<int[]> runs(String x) {
        List<int[]> out = new ArrayList<>();
        for (char ch : x.toCharArray()) {
            if (!out.isEmpty() && out.get(out.size() - 1)[0] == ch) {
                out.get(out.size() - 1)[1] += 1;
            } else {
                out.add(new int[] {ch, 1});
            }
        }
        return out;
    }

    private boolean stretchy(List<int[]> target, String word) {
        List<int[]> r = runs(word);
        if (r.size() != target.size()) {
            return false;
        }
        for (int i = 0; i < r.size(); i++) {  // walk both run lists together
            int c1 = target.get(i)[0], n1 = target.get(i)[1];
            int c2 = r.get(i)[0], n2 = r.get(i)[1];
            if (c1 != c2 || n1 < n2 || (n1 != n2 && n1 < 3)) {
                return false;  // different letter, too short, or an extension shorter than 3
            }
        }
        return true;
    }
}

What the code is doing, line by line:

  1. Run-length encoding turns the two-pointer walk into comparing pairs.
  2. A group can only be extended to a total of 3 or more, never shrunk.

Dry run: use the Step through the solution player under the code. It runs this exact code on Example 1 and shows every line with the variables at that moment.

Edge cases to test:

  • Group of length 2 in s (can't come from length 1).
  • Equal strings (stretchy).
  • Different letters.

Complexity: O(len(s) + Σ word lengths) time, O(len(s)) space.
